did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 29 begins with Job continuing his discourse—that is, continuing his speech and description of his former situation.
Did you know? Job expresses his longing to return to the “months of old,” to the days when God watched over him.
Did you know? Job describes God’s presence through the image of a lamp lighting his path and enabling him to walk even in darkness.
Did you know? In the past, Job would go out to the city gate and take his seat in the street—a place that served as a public and legal center in the life of an ancient city.
Did you know? Job says that those who heard about him and those who saw him testified in his favor, presenting his reputation as widely known.
Did you know? Job describes himself as rescuing the poor who cried out, helping the orphan, and defending those who had no one to help them.
Did you know? Job compares righteousness to clothing he wore, and justice to a cloak and turban—an image emphasizing how deeply these values were part of his identity.
Did you know? Job describes his help for the weak through the images of eyes for the blind and feet for the lame.
Did you know? Job expected to die peacefully in his own home, surrounded by his family, and to live many days like the sand.
Did you know? People waited for Job to speak, listened silently to his advice, and saw him as a leader who could also encourage and comfort.
